deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page): X is a topological space and 𝒢_X is the sheaf of germs of subsets of X. F̲ ⊂ 𝒢_X is a subsheaf satisfying axioms a)–d), which are stated on earlier pages; they are presumably Boolean closure, closure and local-connectedness type conditions on 'tame' sets. F̲ also satisfies a new local finiteness axiom e). Axiom e): for every open U and every decreasing sequence X_1 ⊃ X_2 ⊃ … of closed subsets of U that are sections of F̲ over U, with X_{n+1} nowhere dense ('rare') in X_n, the sequence is locally finite on U. Hence ∩X_i = ∅, and for every quasi-compact K ⊂ U there is i(K) with X_i ∩ K = ∅.

This page then makes four points.
(1) The global sections F = Γ(X, F̲) form a family of subsets satisfying a)–d). F also satisfies the global form of e) if X is quasi-compact, because local finiteness on a quasi-compact space forces the chain to terminate.
(2) More generally, for A ∈ F (or A in the relevant class) one defines F_A. The marginal insertion describes it as the set of subsets of A that are locally traces (or locally sections) of F̲. F_A again satisfies a)–d); whether it satisfies e) is left open ('si ???').
(3) To avoid this difficulty, Grothendieck strengthens e) to a uniform version e_n): there is an integer n such that any chain X_0 ⊃ X_1 ⊃ … ⊃ X_{n+1} as in e), over any U, has X_{n+1} = ∅. This defines 'X is of F̲-dimension ≤ n'. It is a Krull-type dimension via chains of tame closed sets, each nowhere dense in the previous one. It matches the o-minimal fact that the frontier of a definable set has strictly smaller dimension. For A closed in X, every chain in F_A is a chain of closed tame subsets of U, with the same relative rareness. Hence every F_A satisfies e_n), and so e).
(4) NB: F̲ contains the sheaf generated by its global sections Γ(X, F̲), and the inclusion can be strict. Example: the sheaf of germs of analytic subsets of a 2-dimensional complex torus with no nonconstant meromorphic functions. Such a generic torus contains no curves, so its global analytic subsets are only finite sets, ∅ and X. The local germs of analytic curves are therefore not generated by global sections.

The page ends by announcing a new condition f), studied on the previous page, which in the archive order precedes this one.

Purpose: an axiomatic, sheaf-theoretic framework for 'topologie modérée'. A tame structure is given locally as a sheaf of germs of admissible sets, with a dimension theory and stability under passing to closed tame subspaces.
errors: No real error. The F̲-dimension via chains of length n+1 is consistent: with n = dim, a chain X_0 ⊃ … ⊃ X_n can be nonempty and X_{n+1} must vanish.
Gap left explicit by the author: whether F_A satisfies e) without a uniform bound ('si ???'). He sidesteps it by assuming e_n).

The claim that F_A satisfies a)–d) for arbitrary A ∈ F is asserted without proof. The previous page itself notes that stability under restriction to arbitrary (non-tame) opens fails, so 'A ∈ F' (a tame set) is needed.

ideas.what: Tame structures as a subsheaf of the sheaf of germs of subsets, i.e. local rather than global specification of admissible sets
ideas.modern_name: analytic-geometric categories / locally o-minimal structures; local definition of tame (e.g. subanalytic) sets
ideas.usually_credited_to: van den Dries–Miller (analytic-geometric categories, 1996); Shiota; Łojasiewicz/Hironaka for subanalytic sets
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) only calls for tame topology programmatically, without this sheaf axiomatics

ideas.what: Local finiteness axiom e) for decreasing chains of tame closed sets, each nowhere dense in the previous one
ideas.modern_name: finite dimension / frontier dimension inequality in o-minimal geometry; noetherian-type condition

ideas.what: Uniform version e_n) defining F̲-dimension ≤ n, inherited by closed tame subspaces
ideas.modern_name: dimension of definable sets via chains (Krull-type topological dimension)

ideas.what: Sheaf of tame germs strictly larger than the sheaf generated by global tame sets: generic 2-torus with algebraic dimension 0
ideas.modern_name: global vs local analytic subsets; algebraic dimension zero tori have no curves

missed.claim: Grothendieck formulates tame topology locally, as a sheaf of germs of admissible sets with a dimension axiom. He explicitly notes that the local structure need not be generated by global tame sets, using a non-algebraic complex torus as the example. This anticipates the local/global distinction later formalised in analytic-geometric categories (van den Dries–Miller) as opposed to global o-minimal structures. This sheaf-of-germs viewpoint is not usually attributed to him.
missed.quote: NB F̲ est ⊃ le faisceau engendré par F = Γ(X,F̲), et l'inclusion peut être stricte. Ex: germes de parties analytiques d'un tore analytique de dim 2 sans fonctions méromorphes non constantes
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority and framing. It suggests a sheaf-theoretic definition of tame structures on arbitrary spaces, beyond R^n-based o-minimality. Such a definition is still not standard, and a general topos- or sheaf-level notion of 'tame site' remains underdeveloped.

deep.surprise_reason: The page does a careful axiomatic setup of a sheaf-based tame topology with a dimension theory, a decade before o-minimality, plus a nice local-vs-global example. The individual mathematics is elementary and is now standard in o-minimal theory. The novelty is historical, lying in the sheaf framing rather than in any result.
transcription_corrections: 'germes de fonctions analytiques' should read 'germes de parties analytiques' (germs of analytic subsets). This is required for the example to make sense.
'A ∈ 𝔄' is more likely 'A ∈ F' (A a tame set, i.e. a section).
The marginal insertion reads roughly '= ens. des parties de A qui sont loc. [traces?] … des sections de F̲'.
The struck item after 'a) b) c) d)' is likely 'e)'.
In e_n), 'U' is inserted above the line: 'si U, X_0 ⊃ X_1 ⊃ … ⊃ X_{n+1}'.
In the chain of e) on the previous page, the inequalities are 'X_{n+1} rare dans X_n' (nowhere dense).
